rv.q: An intimate, multigenerational drama about a Jewish family in Vienna, set against the tumultuous first half of the 20th century, the play—inexpressibly moving, unavoidably devastating—ranks among Mr. Stoppard’s greatest works.
Across the board, the performances earn your compassion — clearly, a family album in which Stoppard wanted us to invest our most profound sympathies.
Leopoldstadt is a stunning piece of work, gorgeous to look at (as the photos show) and heartbreaking.

Stoppard's deeply personal play about a Jewish family in Vienna across several decades is a moving meditation on memory, identity, and the weight of history.
“Leopoldstadt” is at its best not in instructing us how we must mourn a lost world but in bringing it lovingly back to life.
As a vehicle for recovered memories, and for interrogating the injustice of difference and persistent intolerance, Leopoldstadt is remarkable.

Like The Ferryman and The Inheritance, Leopoldstadt is brilliant, memorable, and dynamic, warranting an immediate visit to the Longacre.
It undeniably ranks, perhaps with Arcadia and The Coast of Utopia, as his most exhilarating, most comprehensive, most serious accomplishment.
Here, Stoppard writes with moving power about finding out the truth about oneself while understanding why that truth was obscured for so long.

'Leopoldstadt' is not just a career-capping work to Stoppard’s stunning oeuvre...but it’s essential viewing for all lovers of theater, history and humanity.

“Leopoldstadt” – bustling with characters, bristling with debate, packed full of facts — is less a collection of distinct portraits or plot points than a rich tapestry of twentieth century Jewish life, and then the frayed threads of Jewish loss.

cn.t: Stoppard's deeply personal meditation on Jewish identity and the Holocaust proves emotionally devastating and intellectually rich, though some find the sprawling cast and complex family dynamics difficult to track.

vs.sum: The Longacre Theatre offers good sightlines with minimal obstructions, even from the balcony, and the sound quality is consistently praised. While the seating is a bit narrow, it provides average comfort for most patrons. The theater's ambiance is enhanced by its elegant Beaux Arts interior, and facilities are typical for a Broadway venue, with some lines at intermission but generally manageable.

acc.note: Small restroom-only elevator (may not accommodate all wheelchairs). 3 wheelchair spaces in Orchestra.
